sections.heading: What is ramipril used for?
sections.body: The NHS describes ramipril as a medicine widely used to treat high blood pressure and heart failure. It is also prescribed after a heart attack, and the NHS says it helps prevent future strokes, heart attacks and kidney problems. The NHS says a person taking ramipril for high blood pressure may not feel any different, but this does not mean the medicine is not working. According to the NHS, ramipril starts to lower high blood pressure within a few hours, but it may take a few weeks to work fully. The NHS says ramipril is generally used long term, and that blood pressure could rise again if it is stopped. Ramipril comes in several forms, including capsules, tablets and an oral solution, which is a liquid. UK patient leaflets say the safety and effectiveness of ramipril capsules in children has not been established. The NHS has separate pages on ramipril side effects, on pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility, and on taking it with other medicines, which can be read alongside this article. MedlinePlus, a US health site, also has a drug information page on ramipril.

sections.heading: How does ramipril work?
sections.body: Ramipril belongs to a group of medicines called ACE inhibitors, the NHS says. The NHS says ramipril relaxes and widens the blood vessels, which lowers blood pressure and makes it easier for the heart to pump blood around the body. StatPearls, a medical reference on the NCBI Bookshelf, says ramipril and its active form, ramiprilat, block an enzyme called ACE. ACE also breaks down a substance called bradykinin, so blocking it raises bradykinin levels, which StatPearls links to the dry cough. StatPearls says the cough usually starts somewhere between a week and six months after an ACE inhibitor is started. UK labelling says high potassium in the blood can occur in people with impaired kidney function or those taking potassium supplements, including salt substitutes, potassium-sparing diuretics, trimethoprim or co-trimoxazole. The same labelling notes that blood potassium usually stays within normal limits, although high potassium may occur in some people.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of ramipril?
sections.body: The NHS describes a dry cough as the most common side effect of ramipril. The NHS says cough medicines do not usually help a cough caused by ramipril. Sometimes the cough gets better on its own if the person keeps taking ramipril, the NHS says. If the cough is bothersome, the NHS says a doctor might suggest changing to a different medicine. StatPearls says angiotensin receptor blockers cause much less cough than ACE inhibitors, which is why they are often used as an alternative. The NHS lists feeling dizzy and headaches among the common side effects, and says the very first dose may make a person feel dizzy. The NHS says to call 999 now if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, or if someone is breathing very fast, struggling to breathe, or has a tight throat or difficulty swallowing. The NHS says swelling of the lips, tongue and face may signal angioedema, and that people with Black skin have a higher chance of getting it. A UK patient leaflet says swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat can happen at any time during treatment.

sections.heading: Taking ramipril with other medicines, alcohol or salt substitutes
sections.body: A UK patient leaflet says that medicines used to lower blood pressure and alcohol can have additive effects. The NHS says alcohol can make dizziness worse, and advises not drinking alcohol until a person sees how ramipril affects them. UK leaflets say anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen can make ramipril work less well. The NHS says daily low-dose aspirin can be taken with ramipril. UK leaflets list spironolactone among the medicines that can increase the amount of potassium in the blood. MedlinePlus advises talking to a doctor before using salt substitutes that contain potassium. UK labelling says ramipril can raise lithium levels in the blood, and that it may lower blood sugar, so people using insulin or diabetes tablets need close monitoring. UK leaflets list sacubitril/valsartan as a medicine to avoid combining with ramipril.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, breastfeeding and who needs extra care
sections.body: The NHS does not recommend ramipril in pregnancy, and says anyone trying to conceive should talk to a doctor first. The NHS also advises planning any pregnancy with a GP or specialist. The NHS says there is no clear evidence that ramipril reduces fertility in either men or women. According to the NHS, ramipril does not affect any type of contraception, but vomiting or prolonged diarrhoea can make contraceptive pills less reliable. The NHS says some hormonal contraception, such as the combined pill and the contraceptive patch, is not usually recommended for people with high blood pressure. On breastfeeding, the NHS says ramipril can be taken, but a person should talk to a doctor or pharmacist first, and it says the medicine is best avoided if the baby was born prematurely. The NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service says ramipril can be used with caution during breastfeeding, but enalapril is preferred, and that this applies to healthy full-term babies only. UK labelling says ramipril should not be used by people with a history of angioedema linked to ACE inhibitors, or with abnormally low or unstable blood pressure. A UK patient leaflet says dialysis or other types of blood filtering may make ramipril unsuitable, depending on the machine used.

faqs.question: Can I drink alcohol while taking ramipril?
faqs.answer: A UK patient leaflet says that blood-pressure medicines and alcohol can have additive effects. The NHS says alcohol can make dizziness worse. The NHS advises not drinking alcohol until a person sees how ramipril affects them. It also says the very first dose may make a person feel dizzy.

faqs.question: Is swelling of the face an emergency?
faqs.answer: Sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue can be a sign of angioedema. The NHS says to call 999 now if this happens. The NHS gives the same advice if someone is breathing very fast, struggling to breathe, or has a tight throat or difficulty swallowing. Swelling in the throat can make breathing difficult. A UK patient leaflet says swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat can happen at any time during treatment.

faqs.question: What if ramipril gives me a cough?
faqs.answer: A dry cough is the most common side effect of ramipril, the NHS says. Sometimes it gets better on its own if the person keeps taking ramipril. The NHS says cough medicines do not usually help, and that if the cough is bothersome a doctor might suggest a different medicine. StatPearls says that after an ACE inhibitor is stopped, the cough usually goes within one to four days, although it can last up to a month.

faqs.question: Can I take ibuprofen or use a salt substitute?
faqs.answer: UK leaflets say anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen can make ramipril work less well. The NHS says daily low-dose aspirin can be taken with ramipril. MedlinePlus advises talking to a doctor before using salt substitutes that contain potassium. UK leaflets also list spironolactone among the medicines that can increase the amount of potassium in the blood.

faqs.question: Can ramipril be taken in pregnancy?
faqs.answer: The NHS does not recommend ramipril in pregnancy. The NHS says anyone trying to conceive should talk to a doctor first, and advises planning any pregnancy with a GP or specialist. It also says there is no clear evidence that ramipril reduces fertility in either men or women.
